',Heron, on October 20th, called the attention of the mem- bers of the Academic dee Scieuces to "Certain Modifications undergone by Glass," which monot be too widely known. G lam is not merely modified when heated to 309 deg. C. •, it underves true deformations at far lower temperatures. The hydronieters used in sugar refineries, by exposure to a tern. perature of B 5 deg. C., are completely modified. Their weight decreases, and they Imeorne erroneous to the extent of 7 deg. or 8 den. B. In chemical works it becomes neces- sary to submit all hydrometers used for hot Aqui& to fre- quent comparison with a standard instrument. Kinn Baannag.—The aseociations of a thousand years cling to Kirk Braddm and instead of the hallowed edifice being "metered," or pulled down, as it might 113113 been if it had been in England, a new church has been erechal close by, without disturbing the dreamy charm arid picturesque beauty of the ancient lane. In the languid summertitne, before this new church existed, the service won wont to he conducted in the open air. The congregation consisted mostly of visitors to the island; and it was 3 strange picture tlut was presented of modern well-dressed idlers mixed up among the wind-rocked trees and mows-grown Scandinavian crossee with their Runic inscriptions. The service was of the quaintest and quietest description, and the preacher was a 'giver-haired clergyman who well might. have sat for the portrait of Oliver Goldsmith'. dear old \ leaf of Wakefield. There was a tender Much of eimplicity in this solemn out. door wordily, among the glancing green of the trees 333 the gloom of the grassy graves, that made one wish to enchant to the epot, instanter, the painters by whom the scene would have been mont sppreciated.—The kagazine if Art. HOW Tan Tut., Snow,. was Ihrtht—lt has been built in 18-inch length of cast-iron tubing, perfectly circu- lar, each 18 inch circle being built up of three segment, with a key-piece at the top, which, lilting in like a wedge, holds the rest with ti.e rigidity oft solid casting. The cast- iron shield used for excavation was lean than teem :kid a half tone weight. 111 front of the shield, which wan slightly con- cave, was an aperture about two feet square, closed With a eliding iron water-tight door, and at the back of the shield were iron sockeM, into which ecrew.jacks fitted, aud, when worked by hand, forced the shield forward. The mode of advance was thia. When a shaft on Tower Hill had been bored to • sufficient depth below the London clay, the shield man lowered and placed in its required position. The water- tight door we have spoken of.. in the centre was then opened. 'Through this aperture suflicient clay, just of the consistency of hard cheese, wae cut away by hand till a nhamher was made large enough for • man, who entered and worked till there was room for two, and these soon made • circular space exactly the aim of the shield and about two feet deep. This dope the miners came out, and with their screw-jacks forced the ehield forwent into the space which they had cut, but with the long telescope-like cap of the shield etill over then,. Under cover of this an 18-inch ring was quickly I-at in and bolted together ; and while this was doing, the clay was being excavated front the front of the shield aebefore. Than every eight hours, night and day, Surulays end week days, the ehield went forward eighteen inchee, and eighteen inches length of iron was added to the tube, which so advanced at the rate of 5 feet 1 inchea every twenty-hmr hoary.-- Wet and See Landon.

With a short hunting.ewonl, while fruitlensly endeavouring to defend himself against the iiifuriated animal, there appeared—con- , tinues the legend—a silver cloud, from the centre of which there came forth a hand, which placed in that of David a eparkling cross of miraculous construction, in ca far that the material of which it was composed could never be discovered. Scared by this interposition, the white stag ded down the hollow way between the hills, hut toof afterwarde slain by Sir Gregan Crawford, whose crest, a etag's head erawd with crosescroaslet between the entices, is still borne by hie descendants, the Crawford, of Kilbirnie, in memory of that eventful day in the forest of Drumsheugh. Thoughtful, and oppressed with great awe, the king slowly wended his way through the forest to the Castle; but the wonder did not , end there, for when, after, long vigil, the king slept, there appeared by his couch St. Andrew, the aposUe of Soothed, Ibc ray. of glory, innrtonctirg bin,, nofonod,npoo 71e rr°47.4t rimS where hr hunt been mir,,cnion,ly centol, twelfth monastery for the canons regular of St. Augustine ; and,M obedience to this vision, he built the nohlenbbey of Holyrood, " in the little valley between two mountains " i.e., the Craig, and the CAW,. Tile Bost. On B, non—The bones of birds are made in quite • different way from there of four-footed animals. These bones, which Imk very ordinary, common sort of bones, are made of layer. upon layer, of a firm elastic sub- stance, and the hollow in the middle it not filled with marrow but with air. If you were to take two inches of the leg-bone of., rabbit. and two inches of the leg-bone of a goose—both measuring about the same in thickness—and weigh them, you would find the bone of the rabbit to se-' -h nearly twice ,

weigh t as Mochas the bone of the goose. Yet the rabbit's bOne you tau snap across, whilst you will certaiuly fail to break the other, be your fingers ever to strong. There is a great bird callod a pelican, common enough in eaatern lands; it intoner- barer five feet high, and twelve feet acrose its expanded wings. It is a water.bird, and can carry in its fishing.bag beneath ita bill a cargo of fish which would Ire sufficient to dine three hungry morn; it can fly fast as it carries thie load home to it. little ones. Yet notwithstanding its great eise and strength, all the bonee in im body do not weigh more than a pound and a half. What make. birds' 1101IPS no light ? Air—air stored in little cells all through the hard substance of the bone itself; and these cells are connected with each other and with the lungs by very ininute tubes. Air-tutee run also to the ends of the quill-feathers. All this air is heated by the natural warmth of the creature, and as warm' are is moth lighter than cold air, birds have a buoyancy something like that of a balloon. Oct has adapted the hollers of each kind of bird lathe mode of life in which Ilia wisdom has placed them. Those that live ganstently upon or near the ground do not poasess nearly so many air-cells as those which dy high and far. Ilave you ever heard of the f r igate- bird, the creature which sleeps and almost entirely lives in the skies 1 It floats upon it. long untiring wing. as lightly as the fleecy clouds which surround it. It hail air-pouches beneath its throat from which it can force warm air between its Orin and its flesh and that supplied it can rest as easily at its Iliazy height as you or I might do upon our beds at home.—Litlle Folks. "Protectionialn" is the name applied to the section of the Tory poly which in IS-14 formed a "Society for the Pro. fection of 'Agriculture " and opposed 411 attempts to repeal the Corn Laws. The leader in this movement was Lord George Bonfinck.mol he was succeeded by the present Earl of Beaconsfield, who now admits protection to be a fallacy.l It was at one time a univcreal custom to "protect " native imlustri, by prohibiting toe it ti,,. of the prmluce of such industries from abroad or by subjecting them to heavy imprat duties. These imposts upon foreign food supplies gave rise to great suffering on the part of (he tNmrer classes in this countrv, and led to the Free Trade movement which remitted in the abolition rot the (..ro Laws in Imo. In con- sequence of the restrictions on the importation of Britieh manufacturers into foreign countries, a Reciprocity Associa. Bon was founded in Manchester in September, 18d9. Its , object was to induce the English Government "recipro- cabs" the commercial restrictions impoe d by the Govern.l merits of tto. countries with whom we trad,sl. At Northwich the apprehensions have been somewhat allayed, althongh another serious subsidence has taken ! phspe on the Dunkirk-road, acmes which the brine is pumped from the beds to the manufactories. The connequence has been to enepend the brine pipes in mid air and to step °peta- -1 tions at all the worke to which these pipes convey Wine. A I short time before the subsidence, horses and carm, with men. were at work on the road repairing danume caused by the former sinking. The land began to crack, the crack widened, and then o large portion of the road went down with an alarming noise. Therein now to be seen thee a great &mem fifty feet in depth. The whole of the neighbouring ground looks as if an mrtl.quake had taken 'lice, accom- , panted by volcanic notion. Small hopes are entertained ' that the Kett'. Hill flock-bolt Mine, dfty acres in extent. , can be worked swain as a rock-salt mine. The water in the shaft had risen on Saturday to a height of eighty yarde. !Peers are entertained that several other valuable rock-sal ! mitten in the neighbourhood will he inundated, and careful , ! watch is beiag kept, and precautions taken. The subter- Irene. effects of the great engulfment of surface water . which has taben place may be estimated by the fact that the ! neighbouring brine beds have had their levels raised seventy- ' six yards. In the Common Pleas Division, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Lindley and Mr. Justice I...pes heard the CAM of Burgess and Another e. the Northwich Local Board. The plaintiffn in this case were owners of him, property in the High-street, .74otthwich. This town was built over a bed of rock salt which was being constantly eaten away by water, and which , water was pumped up in the shape of brine and manufac- tured into salt. This led to a subsidence of the ground, which had been going on for at least 150 years. The houses of the plaintiffs were built in 1870 upon the site of Wm- , house. which had been rendered useless by subsidence, and they were so constructed that they could be rained in one mass by s mechanical c.-.ntrivance when further subeidence occurred. The street watt also, in 1670, restored to what was believed to have been its former levehand this operation ! was repeated in 1872. In October, 1176, the street again subsid...t in some pieces to the extent of five or six feet, and parts of the roadway were flooded. The defendanta raised the street in the best way to meet the requirements of the district and to make a most efficient roadway, and the ! plaintiff, simultaneously rained their 1,. uses. 'the plaietiffs , alleged that what the defendants did was "a raising of the steer'," within the meaning of the Public Health Act, and • they therefore cleirmsl coooopeneetioni bat the defendants ntended that they had merely "repaired and restored " the roadway in fulliini.nt of their duty as surveyors of the , highways. The pla,n,iff.. preceedel to arbitration, which I the defendants to join, and there was awarded to , the plaintiff. /130 for the cost of raining their house, The plaintiffs no at took woceedinaw to recover this amount, and the question now raised upon a special case was whether the defendants were liable. The matter was before the court upon a former occasion, and the Co. was eent back for ; amendment. It was noir returned with a 'statement that the arbitration had found that what WOO done by the defendants .in raising the road non necessary to put it into proper ! !state for traffic, and it could not have been done PS efficiently! without it having been raised cemented in the special case. I Mr. Channell appeared for the ',Waif!, and Mr. Mclntyre, Q C., and Mr. Horace Browne for the defendants. The argument was not concluded when the court row.

SANTA CLAPS FOR POOR CHILDREN. Sir,—The Christmae ems= le =totally looked forward to by Englishmen all over the world, and the feehogs of . children seem common even among older people, and in most boom.' Santa Claus ^ plays no unimportant =.l,e, the joys and festivities of the day. I am, as a School worker, intimately acquainted with some of the poor , chiklren in Manchester. and find that Christmas to hundreds of them. the inost wretched and dreary season of the year. I They eee the 81101.11VilldOW, filled with the toys and lulu- . ries that others are to no jay. If obey play, as they mow, their playthings consist of stones, or pe,thape an old bottle or log of wood, with& piece of string to it ; while at timee they are too hungry anti odd to play at all. For several years a few of the children in Lancashire who we be.= eft and who expect each Christmas a fresh supply of playthings, have packed up all the old toys and picture books wench have done good service in giving them many an hoar'. . amusement, and which they now feel they can spare, and mot them to nee for distribetios on Christer.. morning among boys and girls gathered from the slums of Manches- ter and Salford. Last year 8,800 old and new toys were • thus given to as many children, tec ragged schools taking part in the distribution, and in some cases a good warm breakfast was euujolied in addition to the tors by the kind , contributions of numerous friends. The liitle ones in the Orphan llomes and those liming only to sutler in the Hospitals and Infirmary were not forgotten, and it wee a most enjoyable sight to witness the delight el the little ones as they clutched eagerly at a gaily-dreseed doll or a box of soldiers, it. Now, I would suggest. sir, to other [01•118 that similar work he undertaken, that the poor and rich may alike rejoice together on the Saviour'e birthday. For the poor children in Manchester and Salford I ehall be glad to undertake the distribution of anything your yoteng readers msy send. Parcels of toys (which ehoold each contain the ' name and addrese of sender) or contributions towards <a- nent= will be thankfully received ley Mr. Richard Johan:in, 5, Mosley-street, Manchester. If mat by rail, to be addressed tomcat the Young Men's Christiao Atosodatioo, 58, Peter-street, Manchenter.—Yeara eke, Dec., 1880. GILBERT R. EIRLEC.

Lowleeeness and disrespect of life and limb are Mcreas- log ilarmingly in Ireland ; but though there are deumnde foe theapplieatiun of Ccereive Acts to the Sister I-le there have es yet been no outrages against persons or property committed which the onlinary laws are not adequate to , cope with and redrew. There is undoubtedly a reign of Owror,and it le assuredly the duty of the authorities to put an end to it; but what is required, as it seems to es. is that persons who are made tho victime of outrages shall adopt the ordinary mode of prueeedure in laving complaint., before the authorities, and calling upon them to exercise tha law. " Boycotting " has now brooms the common weapon of the Lend League, and it in being used toe degree that dimmer; Englishmen who have all along sympathised with the land tenantry or Ireland, .tnel evinced a disposition to urge an amelioration of the land biers Captain Boycott, so long as be bore his par..ooll6,ms without lodging ai com- plaint with the authorities, waited in vein for aid , but when he took legitimate eteps for calling upon the authorities to rid him of hie persecutions he found troops of [military and police eent to give hint protection. If people will not take initiatory steps to have the law enforced the law cannot be expected to become cognisant of their need- ing its power. The utterance, of several members of the Mini/dry during the last few days go to prove that the Government is ready cal willing to repress violence and outrage whenever and wherever the exercise of its power is evoked ; Lot it is useless for people, who ore attacked by dastardly assailants, to expect that the law will move of it own accord whilst they cower in a corner and bewail to themselves only their grievances. If the military and con- etabulary forces in Ireland are not sufficiently powerful to checkmate and punish stealthy perpetratora of outrages, the' Government will nod.. slow to increase their strength when ViC6lllB of lawlessness demand the punishment of their &mamas. sltycotting " is, as we have said, increasing its operations, and title week a scandalous case has been brought to light. This plan of pereecation la fostered and en- couraged not only by Land League agitators, but by some of those who profess to be the spiritual guides and ad- visers of the people. This is a specimen of the advice which Canon Doyle gives through the columns of the Wer- ford People to the men of Enniscorthy :—" You have at your dispoul a power hotter than any anny of 200,000 men. It does not require par, clothing, nor support. Care- fully examine in country and town who is your enemy— who is passivety indillennt to your grievances or actively opposed to your redress. Don't touch hint, but Boycott ' him. If he too shopkeeper or publican pass by Lis doer as if the house were infectetkwith a plague. If he hoe brewer or distiller enter. house or groctr's shop where his beer and spirits are sold. Should he have a newspaper, ref nee to SUbber;,... aierVOy it whenever you meet it. ,hould elationer attempt to cell it, by all means Boycott' him Adopt this course, and believe me your enemies will grow ' few by degrees and beautifully leer' in quite a short time. In fast, within one month or lees, the Land Leaguers will be

countlees." With such advice as this ringing in the ears oft dirontented people, it is not to be wondered at that they ehould be found weak enough to adopt it, nor that Mr. Bence Jmles, of Lieselane, county Cork, eboold be nmenkod man, though be Deems to have been One of the considerate and liberal lards of Irish soil. He has been a resident and not an absentee proprietor, and sin, he Inherited his pro- perty, in 1840, he has spent 1,800 a year in permanent im- provetnente. Farming largely himself, he has been paying upwards of .1".5 a week in wages, los labourere' wages vary. log from Bs. to 118. per week, the labourers having in adui- tion a good cottage and garden,and as much land AA they can manure, all free. In Decerntrer hot there was not • shilling owing to Mr. Joces as rent. According to Griffith's valua- tion, his property is worth about lls. per acre, but in consequence of the improvements he Los eff,,cted it now brings in 401. per acre, and his tenantry were sup- posed to be utiefitd. They have, however, been served with notices by the Land League not to pay more than Griffith', valuation, and one morning recently Mr. Jones found that grave hod been dug during the night on hie lawn, for hinteelf and to his eon. The orders for "Boycotting "wore given by the emissaries of the hand League, and Mn. donee found that his labourers declined to work for him, and that no one would buy either hie produce or his live stock. Mr. donee attempted to ship hia cattle to England, but one of the chipping companies was threatened, and it declined Mr. Junee's custom. As the Times pointe out, all the threat. against Mr. Jones, his workprople, his custmners, and the shipping company are off•mces against the common law, and which the common law can retch. But the difficulty is in getting at the criminate, and not in the lack of coercive meaeares which one hears in some quarters no much demand , for. It the parties affected by this last act of .Boycotting" , know who the parties are who have threaten,' them with , pains and penalties, why do not they take the usual 'this- ' , tory eteps for putting the law as it now stands in force, if ' they wish to be rid of the terrorism being exercised over , them? The law cannot compel people to feed Mr. Jones'. live stock or purchase his produce, but it c.m punish them if they use threats or exeroise violence.

It is somewhat dishmrtening, after having en frequently noticed the rather common-place utterances of Mr. Martin Taylor, one of the members of the Yl'idnes School Board, and in [blew ay kept him before the public, to find that he is ungrateful,—like se many mortale to whom you do a favour 1 might have panned him by without notice, or 1 might heve directed toy attention more frequently to other mends., of the body, and then I should, perhaps, have found myself remembered this Christmas fitne. But ingvati- tude has always been our of the crying sine of humanity. I see that he attempu to mub your Widnes reporter," who, I should think, ought rather to be Dunked for the little favours shown. In hiscommunication of the Bth inst., Mr. Taylor states that he does not complain of criticism, but • critic who dares to enter the lisle with him must, amongst other conditions, first show that he understands what he is talking about. lie then proceed, with an attempt to chow that I did not know what 1 wais talking about when I dealt with come of his remarks relating to the District Education Committee. I, therefore, wish to know how it is that Mr. Taylor has acted quite contrary to the magnificent rules by which his conduct's guided in noticing a critic. As I did not fulfil his" conditions," he ot,ht not, according to his own showing, to have noticed met but he lets his seal out- run his discretion, and rushes into print, thereby cleerly proving that at least he cannot " know what he is talking about." Whatever does such a clever man moan by saying "and mound, he may show that he undereUnds what he is talking about," instead, 1 humbly suppose, of "must show ?" I find nothing in your summary of Mr. 'Taylor'. remarks about hie making • competition "between the year. ending Aug. 31st. 1878, and the one ending Aug. 31st, 1890," to which the gentleman says "the upshot " referred. Why doan lie blame me for not referring to what was not in the report? Such a reflection on my observations in most un- just, and, tome than that, it ie perfect', nonwnsiml. Dom Mr. Taylor solemnly mmn to state that trade in Wicks, haa been good during the period which he mentions? lam willing to admit that torn few weeke the trade in chemi.le took a great leap, but thin was very shortly followed by a comparative quietness in the market; and the increawd 1/11111ki never allectel the general body of the ratepayers, as Ire ought modittly to admit. If trade hen been good during the time pained, what was niesnt by the constant complaints unto there being • moot noticeable scarcity of money he all the ehopkeepers ? What mmnt the fact of hundreds of homes being unoccupied. the frequent failures, and the in- ability to get hide at nearly every min of property/ The writer bee only held himself up to ridicule Amongst the ratepayers by making each an amnion in order to establish his position in attacking the work of the committee. Pee' hope Mr. Taylor will In his neat "effort "dory that he haa over said anything reflecting upon that committee ; perhaps he will nay that he hes never irritated the Board by con- stantly going out of his way to make mod t annoying and unmlled for remarks on the Clerk, until at a late meeting the Board had to ask the representatives of the pren not to report him observatione. Emliape he will state that it in not true that he declined on that occasion to permit the Clerk to reply to his attack almut the way in which the bookkeeping wae conducted ? I see from the report on the occasion of the District Education Committee's work being discussed, that Mr. Brunner protested against the committee taing "too ly criticised by members who did not take the trouble to understmd the difficulties the committee had to contend with ;" and the Rev. Mr. Finegan retired from the committee mainly in consequence of Mr. Taylor's unfair attacks. That getttleman does not appear to net that when he in coostantly attacking the resolution of a majority upon the Board all to certain nutters he ie swami.c the time of men of businese; making it appear that their judgment .I.'n throw questions wen otteriY wrong ; not talking for them as if they were a number of children who did not know theW own minds for the space of .me months together.. I understand that a proposal is on foot at Runcorn for leasing land for the erection of small cottagm, which, if carried out, will entirely deetroy the beauty of the coach road in Duke's-field, leading to the river. Leinster gardene formsone of the prettiest rows of property in the town, but if the erection of cottages is carried out by the Bridgewater Trustees, Its vale will be greatly deteriorated. At present all seems very quiet in Runcorn pending the election of members for the School Board ; but I think it will only prove to be the peace •Itich often precedes the storm. The public feeling consequent upon the facts that the Education arepirtment are not at all attislied with the ac- commodation the Board have provided, and that the pur- chase of the Mill Brow school has apparently been a mis- take, Is not of such a description an to bode any good to the retiring members. The advanced section of the Noncon- formists are of opinion that the ratepayers will commit a great mistake if, at the corning election, they return so many gentlemen on the Board who are interested in existing schools It is said that it is not to the iMerest of such re- bresenMtives to disturb in any way the present state of things ; and it is alleged that the ease with which they fell into the proposal of Mr. Preaton to purchase the Mill Brow achpds, proves how willina; they are to let matters remain as they are. If there be 0000000 r, it will originate with the advanced section to which I have referred, who appear to think that the school affairs of town ought to be managed irrespective of the supposed rights of any particular deno• mlnation. tithe ratepayers want a jog-trot etyle of School Board, And are desiroue of being represented by gem] men who may be warranted to do nothiug extreme M any way, butte let things remain as nearly as possible as they are, then their proper course will be to elect the retiring mem- bers, whose motto in a great measure Ippears to be," The thing that has been in the thing that shall he; and "there is .a• a.

The meeting of the Widnee Local Board on Tuesday was one of UntlBll.ll importance. Several cominunications were read from the Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Associa- Ron. One of these indignantly complained of the treat- nient to which the deputation from that body were subjected at the bands of the Chairman (Major Crews) when they attended a previous meeting to lay hare their grievances. Perhaps I may be permitted to say, with all deference to the oftembers of that august association, that it was nut a very prudent thing for them to select as their epokesman, Mr. Allcard, a former servant of the Board. It was not very likely that the Chairman would be conciliated to hear :I surveyor formerly in their employ as- aline such a lofty tone.and attack the Board Self they were banded together for the purpose of doing things which the ratepayers could only view with great suspicion. It would have been far more courteoue to have put forward some one as the chief speaker whose appearance was calculated to in- spire trustfulness, and not to net on tire any latent feeling of irritability. However, Major Cross proved quite equal to giving a reply to such an epistle and he appears to have entirely taken the wind out of the mils of his opponents by mating that he believed the gentlemen concerned did not realty know the meaning of the word ,rourtesy. Re stated as his ground ,for „making thin amertion, previous to the inter- view of the deputation with the Board, he was visited by some of the representative members of the association, and asked to grant than a personal interview for the considera- tion of their complaints. This be agreed to do. but before the day tined upon, the Ratepayers' Association published in some of the pipers circulating in the district, an attack upon the Boanl, which could be characterieed in no other terms than' libellous and outrageous!" This course of proceeding was, without doubt, most imoolitic, and enough to rouse the ire of any gentleman occupying the high position of Major Cross in the district. The Chairman alat argued that the conduct of the representatives of the Aseocia- tion on the day when they appeared at the Local Govern- ment inquiry had been very injurioom to the township, as, owing to their dogged pertinacity in opposing .veral of the revonable requests made 4 the Board, he saw no other course than that of laying an extra rate of one shilling in the pound. This is nice new. for the ratepayers of Widnes, . oleo on' carrying such heavy burdens at present. A long Aug interesting discussion afterwards took place in regard to

the allegol extra,agance el' the Highway Committee. l'hel ' action of the comman was defended by Mr. Foster aed Mr. Barrow, in two able speeches, and it wee apparently shown that tneir financial difficulties had arisen owing to , the Board having tedficed the estiinate which they preeented , to them at the beginning of the official year. : It appears that the pronottal to have an anneal cattle , fair in Widnes has been abandoned. FIALTON MOW., INTROVIOOSST SOClltri.—On Mon. I day, Mr. J. Craig, master of the Collegiate School,Runcern, I gave a humoroue lecture entitled, “Reminiscencee of Scot- tish character." The lecture elicited much laughter from the audience, who were evidently, though not unexpectedly, flighty delighted. Mr. Craig told many of Dean Ramsey's umolotes. He said the habit of getting drunk and of anew- ing was in Scotland at one time considered quite the fashion. In some houses two stalwart men were kept on purpose to carry those guests to bed who had been overpowered with their potations; in others bey was kept to prevert the inebriatea who had fallen under the table from suffocating by untying their neckerchiefs. Many tales were told of faithful servants, and also of parents.- Some of the latter preached the same sermon every Sunday for two or three months; and when they did take snee text the eerroon was ion great measure composed of the one they had preached before. The meeting was very enjoyable, and Racine came too soon for a great nany. Mr. A. E. Davis, occupied the chair. Thanks to the Lecturer and Chairman were unani- mously passed, and briefly acknowledged.—Cow. TliKrr HT A THAN? AT DITTOIf. Ma. Pwrgs RYLAND% the member for Barnley, delivered hie annual addrens to his: constituents on Monday ' night, in the Mechanic.' which was crowded. The hon. gentleman congratulated hie audience upon the improved condition of trade, pointed to the barrennms of Lord Beaconsfield'e costly and dangerous foreign policy, and discussed at some length the Irish question. He enaoreed the saying of Mr. John Bright that force was no remedy, and expressed himself in favour of fined tenure at fair rents, the cultwation of waste lands, and the creation of peasant pro- prietors. The cardinal defect in all previous land legislation for Ireland had been the abaence of adequate protection for the tenant.

Mr. Gladstone, in reply, had admitted the importance of the subject, but said that it was a matter of great difficulty and would require careful coneideration, which he prom' Mtl should be given by the Government. : Ton Dacron Ann WIN Joagn.—The other morning as a belated member of she Owl Club was emering home through the dense fog which the writer is reliably informed hangs ' over this city at three a.m , he passed a house in Mission Street, where resided a well-know physician. The reetibule of this residence was open, amt on its side the dim rays of the moo, struggling through the gloom produced tiy the efforts of the City Gm Company, disclosed the mouth of an acoustic tube, underneath which woe the inscription "Whistle for Dr. Potts." Not wishing to be disobligiug about so mull Smatter, the Owl stumbled up the steps, and steady. log himself against the wall, blew into the pipe with all the etrength of his lungs. The physician who was awakened by the resultant shrill whistle year his head, arose, and after wondering at the singular odour of whisky in the room, groped hie way to the tube, and shouted " Well ?" "Glad to , know you're well," was the reply, "but being a doctor I s'pose toucan keep well at cost price can't you ?" "What to you want ?" mid the man of pills, not caring to joke in , the airy nothing of Ids night-shirt. "Well," said the party at the other end of the tube, after a few moments meditation. "Oh! by the way. are you young Po. or old Potts?" "I am It,. Potts; there is no young Potts." "Not dead,!: hope ?" "There never was any. thong no eon." "Then' you are young Potteand old Petty too. Deat.dearhow sing. What to you want ?" snapped the doctor, who wasl brginning to feel as if his legs were a pair of elongated kicks. "You know old Mrs. Peavine, who lives in the next block ?" " Yes. In she rick? What's the matter ?" "Do You know her nephew, too—Bill Briggs?" "Yes. Well ?" "Well, he went up to Bridgeport shooting this morning, and—" "And he had an accident? Hold up a minute! I'll be right down." "No ; bee all right: brit he got sixty-two ducks--eighteen of 'ant mallards. 1 thought you might like to hear it." And the joker hung on to the muzzle, and laughed like a hyena digging up a fat bullock. 0 1 say," came down from the exasperated M.D., "that's a a jolly good joke, my friend. Won't you take something ?" " What ?" mid the surprieffl humourist,pausing for breath. I"Why, take something. Take this." And before the dis- gusted funny won could withdraw his mouth, a lustily compounded mixture of ink, ipecac, and aseafortirla squirted from the pipe, and deluged bin, from head to foot, about a pint monopolising his shirt front and collar. And while lie danced frantically around sponging himself off with his handkerchief, and swearing like a pirate in the last act, he could hear a voice from above sweetly murmur, "Huge mine more? No? Well, good night. Ceme again soon, you funny dog, you. Bydry."—Baltirriore Tel Nram. The minutes or the Markets' Comrnittee cont.!ined peel. : tioq signed by 17 butcher., which natel that in te.Pearse tee fernier appeal from them the committee decided to place the whole of the butchers' .lltl in the old Market Hall, and thus raised the tone of the meat market by fair WA honest competition. The arrangement had been in force hut a very I abort time, before • successful effort Man triele to alter it, on , , the plea that space was needed for the accomaledation of the ' dealers in batter, eggs, tic. Thil-day's market showed that the agitation enact have been for some other purpose, se not ! a single standing had been occupied by those for whom the I ground was said to he much needed. Farther, the loss of revenue to the market by the exclusion of some of the but. chers' stalls, without any equivalent, ores a matter that might fairly engage the attention of the ratepayers of the borough. The petitioners therefore respectfully asked the committee, in the interests of the market itself, for the bene- fit of the general public, and in justice to the petitioners. toi reetere the butchers' stalls to the Market Hall, and p.m a i bye-law prohibiting the sale of butchers meat in any other portion of the market but the ()Id Market Hall, which they I ' suggested should Lc designated ' The butcher's, or meat market.' Tlietlaan MARTI. then delivered an address. Ile said: I have more than once referred on occasions such as this to the new scheine that was to be framed for the future govern- ment ef this ancient foundation; and it is a great pleaeure to me to be able to seize this last opportunity to introduce it to you. with a few words of explanation and commendation before my connection with Ode school is broken off.. I, for my pert, welcome the scheme heartily, though, by the way, I know that there are some friends present who could hardly be expected to look upon it no favourably as (do. But let me tell you that as regards himself personally, the head master will so far as I can see derive no advintage from it whatever rather the contrary. His position, I say it again, will in seine respects be clearly worse—in no respect. I believe better—than it was under the old scheme. Never- ' tbeless, I have felt for mine years past that the scheme Collid not he, and ought not to be, long delayed, and the sooner it came the better,, fur these reasons In the first place the school could not even maintain it, present very limited number of masters without considerable augmen- tation of ins revenues and an the second place, though I confidently believe, in fact know, iM funds to have been managed and husbanded, as prudently as thom of any Inundation mild be, still there were very erroneous ideas prevalent in the town about its resources, past, present, and future. It was evident that these false impressions could only be dispelled by thorough publicity, and by the admis- sion into the governing body of men whom the represent, tithe borough should think pereonally and especially qoaliliedeneepreetna their views, and to amiat in the, administration of those funds, and to have the general directional school affairs. With respect to the changes to he brought about under the echeme, an far an they will directly affect the convenience :and interests ol the parent, you have probably heard that for the future the year will be divided into three terms of approximately equal length. Two fresh aubjects, namely vocal music and drilling, will be included in the ordinary course of school work. Eight free scholar- ships at least will be maintained in the school, and the scale of fee, will be raised from four guineas and eight guineas to £9 and £l2 is the lower and upper dividons respectively. The adoption of the three terms system will merely involve the addition of a few days to the Easter holidays, and a pro- longation of the stammer term to July instead of June. The result of this will be to aesimilate the system of this school to that of almost every endowed school of like stand. iug with our own. The increase in the fees I Lake. to be a more serious matter. I fear it may press heavily upon many parents who may already be denying themselves little com- forte in order to enure a goad education be their children With such pogo. I have the d!epest sympathy, anti heartily reel,that there want provision in the scheme for such eases. But such is not the idva of educationists now- a-days. Our scheme, like all other schemes, provides that a scholarship shall always he given on the result of com- petitive examination, and as the reward for merit alone. The cleverest boys, wh:ther rich or poor, will be helped— the poor, if not among the cleverest, mut fend for them- selves. This seems very hard, but, at any rate, the trustees and other authoritic, of the school were powerless in this matter. .That, however, tb TO should bran increase in the scale of fees wae tanavoidahle, and I thiek it will be evident to all (rote the fact that during the last six years, although the expenses hare been kept down as much as possible,com- patibly with the efficient wo.king of the school, the eaten- diture has nevertheless exceeded the income by no less th au £7O. per annum. Thie new scheme, which was forced , upon the late trusteee by the Charity Commis-. stoners, %rows the ne7 gov.erfiing body

;;;t:in.' e;t•P'enee's -Which ...I;av;.—been'''hiti;;7o I.7r;i'e by the Head Master personally, and entails a great increme under the heads of tepaira and impreve. 'nem fund, publication of accounts, and other legal kerns, necessitates the employment of additional m esters to teach I ' vocal Inuem and drilling, And requires that at least eight ' boys shall be eduCtled without ptyment of fees. So that, ' ' after a careful estimate of expenses, it is calculated that the cowl have mentioned above will lie the lowest that can be ' reliesa upon to provide for the education that will be given at , this school—such an education as is due to the require- ments cf a populous and prosperous town and neighbour.. hood like that of Warrington. I could well say more on this subject, but I think I have said enough to mmvince any parents who may want convincing of the expeliency of the most practically important changes to be effected by this , scheme. I hope.. shall all be preparet in accept it loyally, , and to give inn fair trial, and I trust that the number ot , those who withdraw their eons in order to give them a cheaper education elsewhere will be very small. I have one , more remark to make, which is to crane from you all, and .pecially from the parents on behalf of my Ettcvstser th I same kind consideration and support that hse been accented Ito me. There will always tw found one or two parents who cannot forget that British idea that the community exists for them, and not they foe the cotnmunity. (laughter.) This feeling is always liable to bring about conflict between such parenM and the bead master, ant the other equally impressed situ sense of the &diem of his position. In such canes an these / entreat your sympathy for the master. When thioo, go on well and smoothly, when the friction of school work is reduced to a minimum, when there is a happy understanding, Ind a spirit of mutual support and muttialgoodwill between parents and master, when he has to do with boys in whose studies and progress he Can tube an intereet and pride, under such circumstances his life ought to hoe happy one, and such has been mine. One cannot hare worked over IT years without a sense or failure in some cases, without a remembrance of some incidents which it would be more pleasant to forget. But tee whole I shall always look tuck upon my work here with thankful. nessand pleasure.
